title: The Prom of the water tower
premise: Odile Okafor, the only out kid in the dying town of Marrow Creek, is counting down to graduation when a college essay prompt—'Describe a moment you couldn't take back'—cracks open a secret: the town's beloved water tower was once the site of a hate crime the whole community agreed to forget, and Odile's own grandmother helped bury the truth. As Odile investigates with the help of Delia Marsh, the sheriff's daughter and their reluctant first love, they uncover records, confessions, and a living victim the town erased. When the essay leaks before Odile can choose whether to submit it, the town turns on them both, forcing a public reckoning at the senior prom held beneath the tower itself. In the end, Odile chooses justice over safety—not by destroying the town, but by refusing to let it stay comfortable—and leaves for college carrying Delia's promise that some stories are worth staying for.
about_author: Zephyrine Amberdale is the pen name of a former small-town librarian who spent a decade cataloguing the things her community preferred not to say aloud. She writes young adult fiction about kids who ask dangerous questions in places built on polite silence.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Lockers
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Senior year begins in Marrow Creek, where everyone knows Odile is 'the gay one' and treats it like weather—unremarkable, slightly unpleasant. Establishes the countdown calendar Odile keeps on their bedroom wall. Emotional beat: weary invisibility mistaken for peace.

chapters.title: The Essay Prompt
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. English teacher Ms. Vann hands out the common app prompt: 'Describe a moment you couldn't take back.' Odile can't think of one, which bothers them more than it should. A throwaway comment from Grandma Ruthie about 'the year of the tower' plants the first seed. Beat: restless curiosity.

chapters.title: Rust and Rebar
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Sheriff's daughter Delia Marsh sneaks cigarettes under the water tower, the town's only landmark, and finds fresh spray paint there: someone has written a name—TOMAS R.—and the word REMEMBER. She paints over it before anyone sees. Beat: guilty complicity.

chapters.title: Assigned Partners
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Ms. Vann pairs Odile with Delia for a local-history project; the class snickers at the pairing. Their first library session is all friction until Odile mentions the tower and Delia goes white. Beat: wary alliance forming over an unspoken thing.

chapters.title: What Grandma Kept
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Going through Ruthie's cedar chest for 'artifacts,' Odile finds a 1974 newspaper clipping with a column cut out, and a key labeled M.C. WATER AUTHORITY. When asked, Ruthie says only, 'Some years don't belong in scrapbooks.' Beat: dread dressed as nostalgia.

chapters.title: The Key Works
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia and Odile use the key to enter the tower's maintenance shed at night and find decades of graffiti layers—and beneath the newest paint, older words scratched deep: names, dates, and 'THEY THREW HIM OFF.' Beat: the past becomes physical.

chapters.title: Tomas Reyes
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Library microfilm reveals Tomas Reyes, a Mexican American teen who fell from the tower in 1974; ruled an accident, never investigated. His family left town within a month. Odile realizes the essay prompt has found its answer without permission. Beat: horror of discovery.

chapters.title: Dinner Interrogation
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia probes her father Sheriff Dale Marsh about 1974 over pot roast; he deflects with practiced ease but later she hears him on the phone saying 'it stays buried.' First hint he may have been a teenager then—or worse. Beat: trust beginning to tilt.

chapters.title: Almost
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Trapped by rain in the tower shed, Odile and Delia share a first kiss that neither acknowledges afterward. The chapter ends with Delia saying 'this doesn't change anything' and meaning the opposite. Beat: love arriving at the worst possible time.

chapters.title: The Town That Forgot on Purpose
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Interviews with elders yield a coordinated wall of 'I wouldn't know about that'—identical phrasing, identical smiles. Odile maps who says what and realizes the forgetting was organized, maybe at church, maybe by the water authority board. Beat: chilling pattern recognition.

chapters.title: Ruthie Breaks
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Confronted with the clipping, Grandma Ruthie confesses: as a teen she saw boys from the tower crowd taunting Tomas the night he died and stayed silent; her father, on the authority board, made sure no one asked questions. 'We decided it was kinder to forget,' she says. 'It wasn't.' Beat: inherited guilt.

chapters.title: Dale's Version
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia finds her father's old yearbook: he was in the crowd photo from homecoming week 1974. He admits he was there, claims he tried to stop it, and begs her to let sleeping dogs lie—for the town's sake, for hers. Beat: loyalty versus truth.

chapters.title: The Living Witness
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile tracks down Elena Reyes, Tomas's younger sister, now seventy and living two towns over. Elena has waited fifty years for someone to ask. She gives Odile letters Tomas wrote describing threats from the sons of the water board. Beat: grief handed over like a torch.

chapters.title: Draft One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile writes the college essay—the whole truth, names included—and can't decide whether submitting it is courage or betrayal of the only home they've known. Delia reads it and says, 'If you send this, we're done being invisible.' Beat: the point of no return approaching.

chapters.title: Leak
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Someone photographs the draft from Odile's backpack—it's posted to the town Facebook page overnight. By morning, nine hundred people know. Delia suspects her father searched her phone; Odile suspects everyone. Beat: violation and exposure.

chapters.title: Small Town, Loud Silence
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The fallout: slurs keyed into Odile's locker, Ms. Vann suspended pending 'review,' Ruthie shunned at the grocery store. But three classmates quietly show up at Odile's table at lunch. Beat: isolation cracking to reveal allies.

chapters.title: The Board Offers a Deal
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. The water authority offers Odile a quiet settlement: retract, apologize, and the town funds a 'memorial garden' with no names. Odile refuses—names or nothing. Dale Marsh warns Delia she's choosing 'that kid' over her own family. Beat: corruption wearing a friendly face.

chapters.title: Elena Comes to Town
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile brings Elena Reyes to Marrow Creek; she stands at the tower and tells reporters the story her brother never got to tell. Half the town watches from porches. Some cry. Some film it to mock. Beat: witness as weapon.

chapters.title: Prom Committee Coup
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The prom, traditionally held in the gym, is relocated—suspiciously—to the fairgrounds near the tower, 'for space.' Odile realizes the board wants a controlled stage for damage control. They decide to run for prom committee to get inside. Beat: turning defense into offense.

chapters.title: Campaign of One
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Delia publicly backs Odile's committee bid, burning her last bridge with the sheriff's department social circle. Her father stops speaking to her except through her mother. Beat: love against duty, made literal.

chapters.title: Ms. Vann's File
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Suspended teacher Ms. Vann slips Odile a folder: old board minutes showing the 1974 'accident review' lasted eleven minutes and was signed by four men—all grandfathers of current board members. Beat: the cover-up has a family tree.

chapters.title: Threats
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Anonymous notes appear in both teens' lockers: KNOW YOUR PLACE. Someone slashes Odile's bike tires. Dale finds the notes, does nothing, and Delia finally calls him a coward to his face. Beat: fear met with fury.

chapters.title: The Second Name
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Elena's letters reveal Tomas wasn't alone—a second boy, Black classmate Curtis Boone, was beaten the same night and fled north, never to return. Odile adds his name to the growing list. The crime wasn't one night; it was a season. Beat: scope widening.

chapters.title: Midnight Archive Run
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile and Delia break into the county records office and photograph the sealed coroner's report: injuries inconsistent with a fall. On the way out they're nearly caught by a deputy—Dale covers for them, visibly shaken. Beat: law bending toward conscience.

chapters.title: Ruthie Testifies to Herself
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Ruthie writes a sworn statement naming the four men she saw that night, including Odile's own great-grandfather. She hands it to Odile: 'You shouldn't inherit my silence.' Beat: generational debt repaid in paper.

chapters.title: The Board Fights Dirty
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. The board threatens Odile's college acceptance via a friendly admissions contact and floats truancy charges. Delia leaks the threat to a regional journalist, Nadia Okafor—no relation—who starts asking questions from outside. Beat: escalation beyond the town's borders.

chapters.title: Split
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Under pressure, Odile and Delia fight: Odile wants to burn everything down; Delia wants to protect what's left of her father. Delia says the cruelest true thing: 'You get to leave. I have to live here.' Beat: first real rupture.

chapters.title: Alone With the Draft
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile, grounded and friendless-feeling, rereads the essay and almost deletes it. Ruthie sits with them and reads it aloud, weeping, then says: 'Send it. Not for them. For the boy who fell.' Beat: resolve reforged in solitude.

chapters.title: Delia Chooses
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. Dale asks Delia to publicly denounce Odile at prom to save the family name. Instead she copies her father's old case files—the ones he kept 'just in case'—and gives them to Nadia the journalist. Beat: duty redefined as truth-telling.

chapters.title: Reconciliation in the Shed
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile and Delia meet at the tower shed, apologize in the language of shared secrets, and plan together: at prom, they'll read the names aloud during the dance, whatever it costs. Beat: partnership restored, stakes doubled.

chapters.title: Prom Night Begins
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Fairy lights strung on chain-link, a banner reading ONE TOWN, ONE FUTURE. The board watches from folding chairs. Odile, in a suit they sewed patches onto, walks in holding Delia's hand. Beat: visibility chosen, terror and all.

chapters.title: The Names
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. During the slow song, Odile takes the mic and reads Tomas Reyes and Curtis Boone's names, the date, and the words THEY THREW HIM OFF. The band falters. Half the gym goes silent; someone cuts the sound—but the room heard it. Beat: climax ignites.

chapters.title: Confrontation Under the Tower
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The board chairman confronts Odile outside; Dale Marsh steps between them and, before the whole town, admits what he saw in 1974 and resigns on the spot. Delia takes her father's hand. Beat: the law finally standing outside itself.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Hour One
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Chaos and strange grace: classmates who never spoke defend Odile to angry parents; the pastor announces an apology service; someone starts pulling ivy off the tower base to reveal the old graffiti. Beat: a town cracking open toward light.

chapters.title: Hearings and Headlines
chapters.summary: Delia's POV. The state opens an inquiry; the coroner's photos go national; Nadia's piece runs titled 'The Water Tower Remembers.' Two elderly men implicated turn themselves in; one dies before charges. Beat: justice arriving late but arriving.

chapters.title: The Garden With Names
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The board's replacement—several resigned—approves a memorial with full names, and Elena Reyes cuts the ribbon, flanked by Ruthie. Odile reads the dedication they wrote. Beat: mourning made public, shame made shared.

chapters.title: Acceptance Letter
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The college accepts Odile—with a note that the essay 'was exactly what we hope for.' Odile realizes they no longer need the countdown calendar and takes it off the wall. Beat: escape transformed into departure by choice.

chapters.title: Graduation
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile gives the senior speech, not about the scandal but about the difference between leaving and fleeing. Delia announces she's staying for community college and the sheriff's civilian aide program—her town, reclaimed. Beat: two futures, deliberately different.

chapters.title: Last Night at the Tower
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Odile and Delia climb the tower's catwalk one last time, the town lights below, and promise each other that distance won't be erasure. They add their own initials beside Tomas's name in chalk—visible, permanent. Beat: love outlasting geography.

chapters.title: The Essay, Final Draft
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, epilogue-style. Framed as the finished college essay itself, Odile answers the prompt: the moment they couldn't take back was choosing to be seen. The last line addresses Tomas directly: 'They remembered you wrong. We're fixing that.' Beat: memory, love, and justice braided shut.
